newsitem.title: KENYA: Confused motives of hijackers that killed 125.
newsitem.headline: Confused motives of hijackers that killed 125.

text.p: The identity and motives of the African hijackers who seized an Ethiopian Airlines plane, causing 125 deaths, remain a mystery more than a week after one of the deadliest acts in the history of air piracy.

But accounts by the two pilots and other survivors paint a picture of three young men from the Horn of Africa with a strong grudge, a slender grasp of geography and eventually a readiness to kill a plane-load of innocent people when their plans went awry.
They were low-tech hijackers, frighteningly so for air travellers who take reassurance from the x-ray machines and body searches at the world's airports.
Almost certainly without any firearm or explosive device in their possession, they seized flight ET 961 at about 11.20 A.M. (0820 GMT) on November 23 after take-off from Addis Ababa.

They kept control for nearly four hours before the pilot, Captain Leul Abate, ditched into the sea just off the Comoro Islands with such skill that 50 of the 175 passengers and crew lived to tell their nightmare.
The hijackers, who remained standing until the end, are presumed to have died in the crash.
A week after the disaster the airline said it had no news about the plane's "black box" flight recorder, had not identified the hijackers and had no idea of their motive.
After suffering two hijackings on internal Ethiopian flights, the 42-year-old captain knew what lay ahead when the men rushed into the cockpit, shouting.
"They said 'We want to go to Australia for political asylum, otherwise we will blow the airplane up,'" Leul told Reuters in his room in a private hospital in Nairobi.
"We know this is a Boeing 767 and it can fly for 11 hours," one of the hijackers said as co-pilot Yonas Mekuria was beaten and ejected from the cockpit.
Slowly, the captain explained about distances and fuel and the need to make stopovers if their ambition to seek political asylum was to be achieved.
"After some argument I think they understood we could not go to Australia (without stops)," Leul recalled.
First reports by survivors suggested they had no message or political agenda at all but this was not quite accurate.

"A few minutes after they took over one of the hijackers went on the public address system and gave a statement first in Amharic, then quite good French and then in broken English," said survivor Kanaidza Abwao, a young Kenyan hotel executive.
Abwao does not speak Amharic, one of Ethiopia's official languages, but remembers what was said in French, which she speaks and understands well.
"The hijacker said: 'There is a problem with the government. We were prisoners and now we have changed the destination.
"'If anyone tries to attack us we are going to blow the plane up. I have a grenade'", Abwao said. She escaped with a broken hand.
That was the only announcement they made.

Survivors say they were in their mid-twenties, resembled Ethiopians or maybe Somalis, and did not move from the cockpit and first-class cabin. They spoke to each other in French. They began what was scheduled to be a journey westwards across Africa in the back of the plane.
"I was in row 26 but I had moved there to sit next to a friend just after take-off," said survivor Mohamed Mirali.
"The three hijackers were sitting further behind because they rushed up the aisles past us towards the front. One...was holding something in his hand.
"He said 'I have a bomb in my hand. Bomb, bomb, bomb'. They were young, in their mid-twenties," said Mirali.
Captain Leul believes that what one hijacker claimed to be a grenade or small bomb was nothing of the kind. But his emergency training told him to concentrate on flying, not fisticuffs.

Survivors' accounts confirm that the hijackers were armed with the plane's axe and fire extinguisher. The two in the cockpit drank heavily and their minds were probably befuddled when their Australian dream started slipping away.
They refused to land in Kenya and ordered the pilot to fly east, across the vast Indian Ocean.
They told him not to descend below 39,000 feet but Leul showed them the fuel gauges heading for "Empty" and made for the nearest land, the tiny Comoro Islands. One engine blew out because of no fuel.
The only announcement during the hijacking, apart from the initial one by the hijackers, was made by Captain Leul at exactly 3 p.m. (1200 GMT).
"He said in English 'one engine is finished and the second engine is running out of fuel. Prepare for a crash landing'" Mirali told Reuters.
Mirali can time the warning because he looked at his watch.
Many passengers said prayers. Abwao asked the Frenchman next to her in seat 34D, right at the back, if she could hold his hand. Everyone put on life-jackets except the hijackers.
As Leul went below 25,000, hoping to land at Moroni airport, the main hijacker said "If you go any lower we will blow up the plane" and wrestled with the pilot to take the controls.

"I said: 'Listen, guys, we're all dead people, there is no argument now'. He was struggling, interfering with the controls. In the last two minutes my first officer rushed into the cockpit and he assisted me in the final ditching of the airplane."
By this time they were suicide bombers without a bomb.
"At the start I think it was a genuine hijack but when they knew that was impossible I think it turned into a suicide," Leul told the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC).
